docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is a Python library that provides a minimal event system for Machine Learning. It allows you to customize code by adding pieces of code that are executed when an event is fired. minevent is organized around three main concepts:

  • event which is a case-sensitive string that names something that happens.
  • event handler which is a callable to execute when the event happens.
  • event manager (EventManager) which stores the event handlers and triggers the events.

A trigger can pass data to the handlers in a read-only Context, a condition can decide if a handler runs, and each registration returns a Subscription that removes it. minevent has no dependency and is fully typed.

A handler is a plain callable, so it can be tested without the event manager, and there is no base class to extend.

!!! note "Version"

The documentation of the `main` version describes the code of the `main` branch. Version `0.5.0`
and older have a different API: use the version selector of their documentation, or see the
[changelog](https://github.com/durandtibo/minevent/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) to migrate.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
minevent provides a minimal event system to customize a piece of code without changing its implementation. Below is an example on how to use minevent library.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def say_something(manager: EventManager) -> None:
...     print("Hello, I am Bob!")
...     manager.trigger_event("after")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
>>> def hello_handler(_) -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("after", hello_handler)
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
Hello!

It allows you to customize the function say_something without changing its implementation.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While minevent is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading minevent to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of minevent.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: This page describes the parts of minevent, what happens when you register a handler and trigger an event, and the behavior that you can rely on. The reasons of these rules, and their trade-offs, are on the design choices page. The quickstart is the first contact, the examples are runnable recipes and the user guide gives the recommendations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Name Role event A case-sensitive str that names something that happens. Handler A callable that runs when the event happens, called as f(context). EventManager Stores the registrations and triggers the events. Subscription The registration of one handler to one event: it holds the options and remove. Context The read-only payload of one trigger. Condition A synchronous function that returns a boolean and decides if a handler runs. PeriodicCondition A condition that is True on one call in freq.

These six names (all but "event") and __version__ are what minevent exports. The public API is what minevent exports: the other names of its modules, such as the functions of minevent.calls, can change. EventManager has the following members:

Member Use add_event_handler(event, handler, *, once=False, condition=None) Register a handler. on(event, *, once=False, condition=None) Register a function with a decorator. trigger_event(event, context=None, /) Run the handlers of an event. atrigger_event(event, context=None, /) Same, and await the coroutine handlers events, get_subscriptions(event), event in manager Look at the registrations. clear_event(event), reset() (and remove() of a Subscription) Remove registrations.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
add_event_handler does the following, once:

  1. It checks that the event is a str, that the handler and the condition (if any) are callable, and that once is a bool (not 1 or "yes").
  2. It reads the signature of the handler and of the condition, and rejects one that cannot be called with the context (see the calling rule). It also rejects a generator function, and a coroutine function used as a condition. A callable object is judged by its __call__. It remembers whether the handler is a coroutine function.
  3. It creates a Subscription and appends it to the registrations of the event.

Every rejection is a TypeError that says which argument is wrong, and it leaves the manager unchanged. The same callable can be registered several times: each call returns a new Subscription, and each registration runs and is removed on its own.

The registration lasts until subscription.remove(), the end of a with subscription: block, clear_event, reset, or, with once=True, the first call of the handler.

docs.title: Trigger
docs.text:
trigger_event(event, context)
    |   take a snapshot of the registrations of the event
    |   build one Context from the context (a Context is used as is)
    |   trigger_event only: a coroutine function as handler in the snapshot -> TypeError
    v
for each registration of the snapshot, in registration order:
    removed since the snapshot?          -> skip
    has a condition that is False?       -> skip
    removed by its condition?            -> skip
    once=True?                           -> remove the registration, or skip if already removed
    call handler(context)
    the handler returned an awaitable?   -> trigger_event raises, atrigger_event awaits it

If a condition or a handler raises, the trigger stops: the exception reaches the caller, and the next registrations are skipped. Triggering an event that has no handler does nothing (the event and the context are still checked).

docs.title: The Calling Rule
docs.text:
A handler and a condition are always called as f(context), with the read-only Context of the trigger. Exactly one parameter must lack a default, and it must be positional: it receives the context. The other parameters keep their default. A condition returns a boolean. The rule is checked once, at registration.

Parameters without default Example Result one, positional def g(context), def g(_) g(context) one, positional, then defaults def g(context, verbose=False) g(context) one, left by a partial partial(save, "model.pt") save(path, context) none: no parameter def g() TypeError none: only parameters with defaults def g(context=None), model.train TypeError *args, with or without **kwargs print, Mock(), AsyncMock() TypeError **kwargs def g(**kw) TypeError cannot be inspected max, dict.update TypeError two or more def g(a, b) TypeError one, keyword-only def g(*, epoch) TypeError (any) generator or async generator def g(context): yield TypeError

Names and annotations are not checked. Coroutine functions, bound methods, callable objects, classes and functools.partial objects follow the same table. The signature is the one that inspect.signature reports: the signature of a partial does not contain the positional arguments that it binds, and a decorator that uses functools.wraps has the signature of the wrapped function. For the generator and coroutine checks, a callable object is judged by its __call__ (a partial by its function): an object whose __call__ yields is rejected like a generator function.

A handler that does not need the context declares it and ignores it: def save_model(_) is the recommended form. To register a function that cannot be changed, wrap it in a lambda:

manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", lambda _: model.train())  # an existing function
manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda context: print(context))  # print the context
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: save("model.pt"))  # save(path)
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(log, "log.txt"))  # log(path, context)

A lambda costs two things: the notes and the repr show <lambda>, and a coroutine function behind it is only detected after its call by trigger_event, once the earlier handlers have run.

In a test, unittest.mock.create_autospec(func) replaces Mock(): it has the signature of func.

A lambda created in a loop reads the loop variable when it is called, but a default value is evaluated when the lambda is created. So lambda _, i=i: print(i) saves the current value: the context comes first, without default.

docs.title: Events and registrations
docs.text:
• An event name is a case-sensitive str. A StrEnum member is a str, and is kept as given. The empty string is valid. The methods of the manager raise a TypeError for another type, while in answers like a dict (1 in manager is False).
  • Reading the manager never creates an event: events lists the events that have at least one registration.
  • subscription.remove() removes that registration only. It returns True the first time, then False. subscription.active is True exactly while the registration is in the manager, so it becomes False when the registration is removed, by whatever means. A Subscription cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise a TypeError), and the manager alone creates one.
  • The repr of a Subscription shows what decides whether its handler runs: after the event and the name of the handler, once=True, the name of the condition and active=False, each only if it applies.
  • bool(manager) is always True, empty or not, and a manager has no length: the number of handlers of an event is len(manager.get_subscriptions(event)), and repr(manager) shows it for each event. A manager cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise a TypeError).

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
• The handlers of an event run in the order they were registered, one after the other, in the calling thread.
  • A trigger visits the registrations that exist when it starts. A registration added by a running handler takes effect at the next trigger. A registration removed before its handler is called (by remove(), clear_event, reset or a once claim) does not run, whoever removed it: another handler, or its own condition.
  • A condition is called just before its handler, so it sees the effects of the handlers that ran before.
  • A once registration is removed by an atomic claim just before its handler is called, after its condition, so it is called at most once whatever the number of threads. A false or raising condition does not consume it; a handler that raises does.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
• trigger_event(event, context) copies the mapping context (a dict, for example), or reuses a Context as is, into one read-only Context per trigger, shared by the handlers and the conditions. Both arguments are positional-only.
  • Any str key is allowed, it does not need to be a valid identifier. Another key raises a TypeError. The mapping is read once: the keys that are checked are the keys that are stored.
  • The values are not copied. A Context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (protocol 2 or higher) if its values can.
  • A Context is equal to a mapping that has the same items, and it is not hashable.
  • Context is final (typing.final): a type checker reports a subclass, and nothing changes at run time.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• An exception of a handler or a condition propagates unchanged (same object, same type), and the remaining handlers are skipped. Python makes one exception to this: a StopIteration leaves atrigger_event as a RuntimeError (see Limits).
  • An Exception carries a note with the event and what raised it: the handler, or the condition and its handler (each named by its function, under a functools.partial). The same note is not added twice. An exception that cannot take a note (a frozen dataclass exception, for example) propagates without it. A BaseException that is not an Exception, such as KeyboardInterrupt or asyncio.CancelledError, has no note.
  • The messages of minevent do not run the repr of your objects to name a callable. Naming one never raises in place of your exception: the name of its class is used if its own name cannot be read.
  • The messages and the notes of minevent stay short whatever the size of your data: a value is shown with reprlib, an event name is shortened above 200 characters, and the KeyError of a Context lists at most 20 keys.

docs.title: Coroutines
docs.text:
• trigger_event never awaits. If a registration of the snapshot has a coroutine function as handler, it raises a TypeError before any condition or handler runs, whatever the conditions would answer. Any other handler that returns an awaitable raises a TypeError after its call.
  • atrigger_event awaits what a handler returns, if it is awaitable, before it calls the next handler. It also runs the synchronous handlers.
  • Conditions are synchronous in both: a coroutine function, or an object whose __call__ is one, is rejected at registration, and a condition that returns an awaitable raises a TypeError at the trigger.
  • A coroutine that is rejected is closed, so it does not emit a "never awaited" warning.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
• Registering, removing, triggering and reading the manager are safe from several threads, with and without the GIL.
  • Your code (handlers, conditions, repr and the finalizers of the removed handlers) runs outside the lock of the manager, so it can use the manager. The lock protects the manager against the other threads only: a signal handler or a garbage collection finalizer must not change it (see Limits).
  • PeriodicCondition counts every call once, from any number of threads. It can be copied and pickled: a copy starts at the same step and has its own counter. Its step property reads the number of calls since the creation or the last reset(), without advancing the counter. Its repr shows freq, start and step as Python writes integers, without separator.

docs.title: Import and typing
docs.text:
• minevent uses the standard library only. import minevent starts no thread, emits no warning and writes no output and no log. It reads __version__ from the metadata of the installed package.
  • The package is fully typed (py.typed). A handler argument is typed Handler, so a type checker reports a function without parameter, or a callable that needs two arguments, a keyword-only argument or an argument of another type than Context. The run-time check of the calling rule stays the authority. The values of a Context are typed Any.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
minevent does not protect against the following:

  • A removal in another thread cannot stop a handler whose trigger has already checked that it is registered.
  • A signal handler or a garbage collection finalizer can interrupt a method of the manager in the same thread. One that adds, removes or triggers a once registration can make remove() raise, or leave a subscription active that is not registered. Set a flag in it, and use the manager in the main code.
  • Concurrent calls. A registration without once is called by every thread that triggers its event, possibly at the same time. A handler or a condition of yours that shares state must protect it.
  • Recursion. A handler that triggers its own event recurses until RecursionError.
  • Blocking. A synchronous handler in atrigger_event blocks the event loop.
  • StopIteration in atrigger_event. A coroutine cannot raise it, so Python turns the one of a handler or a condition into a RuntimeError, whose __cause__ is the original exception and has the note.
  • The start of a coroutine. atrigger_event reads the registrations and copies the payload when its coroutine starts to run, not when it is created: a task sees a change made to the dict, or a handler added, before it starts. To fix the payload at the creation, give it a Context, which is copied when it is built.
  • A hidden coroutine. A lambda, or a synchronous functools.wraps wrapper, that returns a coroutine is only detected after its call by trigger_event: the handlers before it have run, and a once registration is consumed.
  • A cached function. functools.cache and functools.lru_cache hash their arguments, and a Context is not hashable: such a handler or condition raises a TypeError at the trigger.
  • Hidden generators. A function that returns a generator or an asynchronous generator, such as a lambda that calls a generator function, does nothing.
  • A signature that depends on Python. The standard library adds signatures to C callables between versions: set().add and time.sleep are rejected on Python 3.11 and 3.12, and accepted from 3.13.
  • A condition is evaluated by truthiness, and counts its calls, not the triggers. It is not called when an earlier handler raised, nor for a removed registration.
  • Names are not checked. An unbound method such as Model.save has one parameter without default, self, so it is accepted and called with the context as self.
  • A huge integer in a message on Python 3.11 and 3.12: showing an integer of more than 4,300 digits (a value given as a handler, a key, an argument of PeriodicCondition) raises the ValueError of Python instead of the error of minevent.
  • A mutable value of the payload can be mutated by a handler, and the next ones see it.
  • Delayed release. A manager with registrations is in a reference cycle (manager, registry, Subscription, manager): del manager does not free it until the garbage collector runs. reset() releases the handlers at a known point.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
The registry maps each event to an ordered dict of subscriptions, used as an ordered set:

  • registering and removing a handler are O(1), whatever the number of handlers;
  • a trigger is linear in the number of handlers of its event, and the other events cost nothing;
  • the signature is inspected at registration, never during a trigger;
  • a mapping given to a trigger is copied (linear in its number of keys), while a Context is not;
  • context.get(key, default) and key in context cost the same for a present key and a missing one. context[key] lists up to 20 keys in its KeyError, so a missing key costs more.

As an order of magnitude, measured on a laptop with Python 3.14: about 0.3 µs for a trigger with one trivial handler, 0.07 µs for each extra one, 0.8 µs with a small dict, and 5.5 µs for a registration plus its removal. Measure on your machine with inv test.benchmark in a source installation.

docs.title: Design Choices
docs.text: minevent is built to stay small: it routes an event to the code that you attached to it, in a predictable order, and does nothing else. This page explains the main choices, what they give you and what they cost, so you can decide if they fit your program and work with them. The rules themselves are on the how it works page.

docs.title: Events are strings
docs.text:
An event is a str, not an object.

  • Benefits: nothing to declare or import to emit an event, names are easy to read, log and serialize, and any part of a program can agree on a name.
  • Costs: a typo is silent, because triggering an event without handler is valid. There is no hierarchy or wildcard: training.batch.end is only a naming convention, and the data of an event goes in the payload, not in the event.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about events.

docs.title: A handler is a plain callable
docs.text:
There is no base class or protocol to implement, and a condition is a function too.

  • Benefits: any function, method, lambda, functools.partial or callable object works, and a handler can be tested without a manager. There is one way to extend the library: write a callable.
  • Costs: the library cannot attach a name, a priority or metadata to a handler. A mistake in a signature is found at registration (or by your type checker), not by an interface.
  • In practice: use a class with __call__ when a handler needs a state.

docs.title: A handler is always called with the context
docs.text:
A handler and a condition are called as f(context) (the calling rule). The signature is checked once, at registration.

  • Benefits: there is one call to learn, and a context is always there. Adding or removing a default never changes the call, and a callable that cannot be called is rejected immediately, before a long training.
  • Costs: a function that does not need the context declares it anyway, or is wrapped in a lambda, so model.train is not registered as it is. Callables that accept *args (print, Mock()) or cannot be inspected are rejected, even when a call would work.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about handlers.

docs.title: The payload is one read-only Context
docs.text:
The data of a trigger is passed as one Context, not as keyword arguments.

  • Benefits: handlers of the same event can read different keys, adding a key to a trigger breaks no handler, each handler decides what a missing key means, and no handler can add, replace or remove a key seen by the next one.
  • Costs: the signature of a handler does not list the data that it needs, a typo in a key is found at run time, and a dict is copied at each trigger. Context is final: it is data, so build one from your mapping, or wrap it, instead of subclassing it.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about the payload.

The protection is shallow: the values are not copied, because copying arbitrary objects (a model, a tensor) is expensive or impossible. A mutable value can be changed by a handler; take a copy.deepcopy if you need a snapshot.

docs.title: The values of a Context are typed Any
docs.text:
• Benefits: a handler computes with a value (context["epoch"] + 1) without a cast.
  • Costs: a type checker does not check the keys or the use of the values.
  • In practice: annotate the variable that receives a value (epoch: int = context["epoch"]), or check it at run time, if you need more safety.

docs.title: A registration is an object
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, and there is no method that removes a handler by comparing callables.

  • Benefits: the same callable can be registered several times with different options, a removal is exact and O(1), including for lambdas and partials that you cannot compare, and a with block scopes a registration.
  • Costs: you must keep the Subscription if you want to remove it later, and an object that holds one cannot be copied or pickled as it is: a copy would describe a registration that does not exist.
  • In practice: otherwise, search the result of get_subscriptions(event) for your handler.

docs.title: A trigger works on a snapshot
docs.text:
The registrations are read when the trigger starts. An addition waits for the next trigger, while a removal applies immediately.

  • Benefits: a handler can add or remove handlers without changing the list that is being visited, and a handler that registers another one cannot loop forever. A removed handler does not run any more, even if its own condition removed it.
  • Costs: a handler cannot extend the current dispatch.
  • In practice: trigger another event if some work must happen immediately.

docs.title: A trigger stops at the first error
docs.text:
An exception of a handler or a condition reaches the caller unchanged, with a note, and the next handlers are skipped.

  • Benefits: errors are never hidden, the traceback and the type of the exception are the ones of your code, and the dispatch has no error policy to configure.
  • Costs: one failing handler prevents the next ones from running, and there is no option to collect the errors into an ExceptionGroup.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about handlers.

docs.title: Handlers run one after the other
docs.text:
A trigger is synchronous and sequential. Coroutines are opt-in with atrigger_event, which awaits them one at a time, and the library starts no thread.

  • Benefits: the order is deterministic, a handler can rely on the work of the previous one, which suits the sequential workflows of Machine Learning, and it is easy to debug.
  • Costs: a slow handler delays the next ones and the caller, handlers do not run concurrently, and a synchronous handler blocks the event loop.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about handlers.

docs.title: A synchronous trigger rejects coroutine handlers first
docs.text:
trigger_event looks for a coroutine function among the handlers before it runs anything.

  • Benefits: a trigger does not stop in the middle, no once registration is consumed, and the mistake appears at the first trigger, not at the first one where a condition is true.
  • Costs: one more pass over the handlers at each trigger, and a coroutine handler whose condition is false rejects the trigger too.
  • In practice: see the troubleshooting of coroutine handlers.

docs.title: Conditions are synchronous
docs.text:
• Benefits: a condition has the same meaning with trigger_event and atrigger_event, and a coroutine, which is truthy, cannot make a handler run by mistake.
  • Costs: a decision that needs I/O cannot be a condition.
  • In practice: see the troubleshooting of asynchronous conditions.

docs.title: once is claimed before the call
docs.text:
A once registration is removed after its condition and just before its handler.

  • Benefits: the handler runs at most once, even with several threads, and a false condition keeps the registration for a later trigger.
  • Costs: a handler that raises is not retried.
  • In practice: for a retry, register without once and call subscription.remove() after the success.

docs.title: The manager is thread-safe, your code is not
docs.text:
A reentrant lock protects the registry only. A trigger takes its snapshot under the lock and calls your code outside of it.

  • Benefits: your code can use the manager, a slow handler does not block the registrations of other threads, and a lock of yours cannot deadlock with the one of the manager.
  • Costs: handlers can run concurrently, and a removal in one thread cannot stop a call that another thread is about to make.
  • In practice: protect the shared state of your handlers and conditions. PeriodicCondition protects its counter.

docs.title: The manager is an explicit object
docs.text:
There is no global manager and no automatic discovery. A manager is always truthy, it has no length, and it cannot be copied or pickled.

  • Benefits: the ownership is visible, tests do not share state, and manager or default means "is there a manager". A copy that silently shares or loses registrations cannot happen.
  • Costs: you pass the manager to the code that triggers events, and an object that holds a manager needs its own rule to be pickled, for example to be sent to another process.
  • In practice: see the troubleshooting of copies.

docs.title: The manager keeps strong references
docs.text:
• Benefits: a registered lambda or bound method cannot disappear unexpectedly.
  • Costs: an object stays alive while one of its methods is registered.
  • In practice: see the recommendations about the manager.

docs.title: Nothing is logged
docs.text:
• Benefits: no configuration, no output that you did not ask for, and no cost on a trigger.
  • Costs: to see which handlers ran, you add the trace yourself.
  • In practice: see how to debug.

docs.title: No dependency and a small surface
docs.text:
minevent depends on the standard library only, so it can be added to any project without a version conflict. It also leaves out features that other event libraries have:

Not provided What to do instead Event objects with metadata Pass the data in the payload. Priorities or ordering rules Register the handlers in the order they must run. Hierarchy or wildcards of events Register the handler to each event. Weak references, filtering by sender Remove the subscriptions; filter with a condition. Collecting the errors of several handlers Catch the exceptions in the handlers. Concurrent or background dispatch Start the tasks or threads inside a handler.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This page shows how to use minevent in practical situations. The pycon examples run as written. The quickstart shows each feature on its own, the user guide lists the recommendations and the how it works page states the rules.

docs.title: Add logging to a training loop
docs.text:
The training loop triggers events and knows nothing about the handlers. The caller decides what happens, so logging, checkpointing or monitoring is added without changing the loop:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def train(manager: EventManager, epochs: int) -> None:
...     manager.trigger_event("training_start")
...     for epoch in range(epochs):
...         loss = 1.0 / (epoch + 1)
...         manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
...     manager.trigger_event("training_end")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_start", lambda _: print("Training started"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}: loss={context['loss']}")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda _: print("Training ended"))
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
Training started
epoch 0: loss=1.0
epoch 1: loss=0.5
Training ended

The first call of train prints nothing because no handler is registered.

docs.title: Run a handler every N epochs
docs.text:
Give the registration a condition. PeriodicCondition(freq=3) is True on the first call and then every three calls. start is the index (from 0) of the first call that is True: start=3 skips the first call:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"checkpoint at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3, start=3),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(7):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
checkpoint at epoch 3
checkpoint at epoch 6

With the epochs counted from 0, start=2 runs the handler at the end of every third epoch:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"evaluate at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3, start=2),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(7):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
evaluate at epoch 2
evaluate at epoch 5

With freq=1, the condition is False for the first start calls, then always True, which is useful for a warm-up:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"validate at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=2),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(4):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
validate at epoch 2
validate at epoch 3

docs.title: Write a custom condition
docs.text:
A class with __call__ is useful when a condition has a state or reads another object:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class Flag:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.enabled = False
...
...     def __call__(self, _: Context) -> bool:
...         return self.enabled
>>> verbose = Flag()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda _: print("batch done"), condition=verbose)
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
>>> verbose.enabled = True
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
batch done

docs.title: Restart a condition
docs.text:
reset() restarts the counter of a PeriodicCondition, for example at the start of a new training:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> warmup = PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=1)
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: print("validate"), condition=warmup)
>>> for _ in range(2):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
validate
>>> warmup.reset()
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

docs.title: Combine conditions
docs.text:
Write a function. all([a(context), b(context)]) evaluates every condition at each call, so stateful conditions advance together:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> after_one, periodic = PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=1), PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda _: print("validate"),
...     condition=lambda context: all([after_one(context), periodic(context)]),
... )
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
validate
validate

docs.title: Use one condition per handler
docs.text:
A stateful condition keeps its counter in the instance, so create one per registration, for example with a function:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> def say(name: str, _: Context) -> None:
...     print(name)
>>> def register(name: str) -> None:
...     manager.add_event_handler(
...         name, functools.partial(say, name), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
...     )
>>> register("first")
>>> register("second")
>>> manager.trigger_event("first")
first
>>> manager.trigger_event("second")
second

docs.title: Decide from the payload
docs.text:
A condition reads the payload of the trigger. A handler and its condition can read different keys:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def is_improving(context: Context) -> bool:
...     return context.get("loss", 1.0) < 0.5
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"save the model of epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=is_improving,
... )
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.4, 0.6, 0.3]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
save the model of epoch 1
save the model of epoch 3

PeriodicCondition ignores the payload. To combine it with a condition on the payload, write a function that calls both: condition=lambda context: periodic(context) and is_improving(context).

docs.title: Keep a state in a handler
docs.text:
A class with a __call__(self, context) method is a handler with its own state. This one collects the losses and is read after the training:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class LossHistory:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.losses = []
...
...     def __call__(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         self.losses.append(context["loss"])
>>> history = LossHistory()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", history)
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.6, 0.4]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
>>> history.losses
[0.9, 0.6, 0.4]

The handler ignores the keys that it does not read, here epoch.

docs.title: Pass a dict or a Context
docs.text:
A dict is copied and validated at each trigger, while a Context is passed as is, so build it once to reuse it:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context['loss']}")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3, loss 0.5
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 4, "loss": 0.4})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4

docs.title: Adapt an existing function
docs.text:
A handler is called with the context, so wrap a function that does not take it, such as model.train, in a lambda that ignores it and chooses the arguments. A default saves the value of a loop variable:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> class Model:
...     def train(self, mode: bool = True) -> None:
...         print(f"train mode: {mode}")
>>> model = Model()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", lambda _: model.train())
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("validation_start", lambda _: model.train(mode=False))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": 0})
train mode: True
>>> manager.trigger_event("validation_start")
train mode: False
>>> for i in range(3):
...     _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda _, i=i: print(i))
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
0
1
2

docs.title: Keep a snapshot of the payload
docs.text:
The values of a Context are not copied. copy.deepcopy takes a snapshot that the next handlers cannot change:

>>> import copy
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> snapshots = []
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: snapshots.append(copy.deepcopy(context)))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: context["losses"].append(0.1))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"losses": [0.5]})
>>> snapshots
[Context({'losses': [0.5]})]

docs.title: Register a handler only once
docs.text:
Registering the same handler twice runs it twice. Look at the registrations to add it only if it is not there:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(_: Context) -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> for _ in range(3):
...     if not any(s.handler is hello_handler for s in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
...         _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

docs.title: Trace the handlers
docs.text:
Wrap a handler to see its calls. functools.wraps keeps the signature, which is checked at registration:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def traced(handler):
...     @functools.wraps(handler)
...     def wrapper(*args):
...         print(f"calling {handler.__name__}")
...         return handler(*args)
...
...     return wrapper
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", traced(log_epoch))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(dict(context)))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
calling log_epoch
epoch 1
{'epoch': 1}

docs.title: Write a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin registers its handlers when it is set up, and keeps the subscriptions to remove them when it is torn down:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class ProgressPlugin:
...     def setup(self, manager: EventManager) -> None:
...         self.subscriptions = [
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", self.on_epoch_start),
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", self.on_epoch_end),
...         ]
...
...     def teardown(self) -> None:
...         for subscription in self.subscriptions:
...             subscription.remove()
...
...     def on_epoch_start(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"start {context['epoch']}")
...
...     def on_epoch_end(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"end {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> plugin = ProgressPlugin()
>>> plugin.setup(manager)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": 0})
start 0
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 0})
end 0
>>> plugin.teardown()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

docs.title: Trigger events from several threads
docs.text:
The manager can be shared between threads. The handlers run in the thread that triggers the event, possibly at the same time, so a handler protects the state that it shares:

>>> import threading
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> total, lock = [0], threading.Lock()
>>> def add(context: Context) -> None:
...     with lock:
...         total[0] += context["value"]
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("item_done", add)
>>> threads = [
...     threading.Thread(target=manager.trigger_event, args=("item_done", {"value": i}))
...     for i in range(10)
... ]
>>> for thread in threads:
...     thread.start()
>>> for thread in threads:
...     thread.join()
>>> total
[45]

docs.title: Trigger events from an async function
docs.text:
In an async program, await the trigger inside your coroutines. The next step starts when every handler is done:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def fetch_all(manager: EventManager, urls: list[str]) -> None:
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_start", {"count": len(urls)})
...     for url in urls:
...         await asyncio.sleep(0)  # a real program awaits a request here
...         await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_done", {"url": url})
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_end")
>>> async def log_done(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"fetched {context['url']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "fetch_start", lambda context: print(f"fetching {context['count']} urls")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_done", log_done)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_end", lambda _: print("done"))
>>> asyncio.run(fetch_all(manager, ["a.com", "b.com"]))
fetching 2 urls
fetched a.com
fetched b.com
done

docs.title: Use options with coroutine handlers
docs.text:
once, condition and the on decorator work the same way with coroutine handlers:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end", condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
... async def upload(context: Context) -> None:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     print(f"uploaded epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> async def main() -> None:
...     for epoch in range(3):
...         await manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": 0.5})
>>> asyncio.run(main())
uploaded epoch 0
uploaded epoch 2

docs.title: Run the work of a handler concurrently
docs.text:
The handlers of an event run sequentially, so a slow handler delays the next ones. To run several awaitables at the same time, use asyncio.gather inside one handler:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def upload(name: str) -> str:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     return name
>>> async def upload_all(context: Context) -> None:
...     done = await asyncio.gather(*(upload(name) for name in context["files"]))
...     print(f"uploaded {done}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", upload_all)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("training_end", {"files": ["a.pt", "b.pt"]}))
uploaded ['a.pt', 'b.pt']

Hand a long computation to an executor (await loop.run_in_executor(...) or asyncio.to_thread) from a coroutine handler.

docs.title: Test a handler
docs.text:
A handler is a plain callable, so test it without a manager. Test the wiring with a mock:

from unittest.mock import create_autospec

from minevent import Context, EventManager


def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
    print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")


def test_epoch_end_calls_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = create_autospec(log_epoch)  # a mock with the signature of log_epoch
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
    handler.assert_called_once_with({"epoch": 1})

An async handler is tested with asyncio.run (or the async support of your test framework):

import asyncio
from unittest.mock import create_autospec

from minevent import Context, EventManager


async def upload(context: Context) -> None:
    await asyncio.sleep(0)


def test_epoch_end_awaits_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = create_autospec(upload)  # an async mock with the signature of upload
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}))
    handler.assert_awaited_once_with({"epoch": 1})

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with pip (recommended)
docs.text:
We highly recommend installing a virtual environment. minevent can be installed from pip using the following command:

pip install minevent

minevent has no dependency, so no optional dependencies or extras are required. It requires Python 3.11 or newer on the main branch (see the version table for the releases). It supports Linux and macOS: Windows is not supported.

This command installs the latest release. Version 0.5.0 and older have a different API than the one of the main documentation. To install the code of the main branch:

pip install git+https://github.com/durandtibo/minevent.git

Check the installation:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("hello", lambda _: print("Hello!"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("hello")
Hello!

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text: To install minevent from source, you can follow the steps below.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This project uses uv for dependency management. If you don't have uv installed, you can install it by following the official installation guide.

docs.title: Clone the repository
docs.text:
First, clone the git repository:

git clone https://github.com/durandtibo/minevent.git
cd minevent

docs.title: Install the dependencies
docs.text:
Create the virtual environment .venv with the package (in editable mode) and its development dependencies, then activate it:

uv sync --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate

To also install the documentation dependencies, use uv sync --python 3.13 --group docs.

Once the environment is activated, inv env.install installs the dependencies again, and inv env.update updates them. inv --list shows all the tasks.

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
Finally, you can test the installation by running the test suite:

inv test.unit --cov

docs.title: Development workflow
docs.text: If you're planning to contribute to minevent, please refer to the Contributing Guide for more information on setting up your development environment and running tests.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide collects the recommendations and the troubleshooting tips for using minevent. The quickstart shows the basics, the examples are the recipes, the how it works page states the rules and the limits of the library and the design choices page explains them.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
• Name the event after what happened, in the past tense: epoch_end, checkpoint_saved, not event1 or done.
  • Pick one convention for the whole project, for example snake_case (batch_end) or a namespace (training.batch.end). Names are only strings, so minevent has no notion of hierarchy.
  • Define the names in one place (constants or a StrEnum) to avoid typos: the events "epoch_end" and "epoch-end" are different, and triggering an event without handler does nothing. A member of a plain Enum is not a str, so it is rejected.

docs.title: Handlers and payload
docs.text:
• One handler does one thing (log, save, update a progress bar). Register the handlers of an event in the order they must run.
  • Pass the data of a trigger as a dict. Build a Context yourself to reuse it for several triggers: it is validated and copied only once.
  • Read a required value with context["key"] and an optional one with context.get(key, default), so that handlers with different needs can share an event.
  • Write def f(_) for a handler that ignores the context, and wrap an existing function in a lambda such as lambda _: model.train() (see the calling rule).
  • If the failure of a handler must not stop the program, catch the exception in the handler.
  • A synchronous handler that is slow blocks the caller (and the event loop in atrigger_event). Hand the work to an executor in the handler if the caller must not wait.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
• Give each registration its own PeriodicCondition: an instance shared by two handlers advances the same counter. Call reset() to restart it.
  • For a warm-up, use PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=n): it is False for the first n calls, then True.
  • To combine conditions, write a function. lambda context: a(context) and b(context) skips b when a is False, so use it when b is costly and stateless. lambda context: all([a(context), b(context)]) evaluates both, so stateful conditions advance together.
  • Use a condition to avoid the work of an expensive handler.

docs.title: The event manager
docs.text:
• Create the manager once and pass it where it is needed. minevent has no global manager on purpose: it keeps the tests independent and makes the ownership clear.
  • Keep the Subscription of a handler that you may remove. A registered handler lives as long as the manager (obj.method keeps obj alive, and so do the arguments of a functools.partial and the closures), and minevent uses no weak reference. Remove the subscriptions that you do not need any more with remove(), a with block, clear_event or reset.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Test a handler without a manager, and the wiring with create_autospec (see Test a handler).
  • Use a new EventManager in each test, or call manager.reset() if the manager is shared.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The cost of a trigger is mostly the cost of the handlers (see Performance). To find a slow handler, time it or wrap it (see Trace the handlers). In a loop that triggers often with the same data, build one Context and reuse it.

docs.title: My handler does not run
docs.text:
1. The handler is registered for that event: print(manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")) lists the registrations of the event, with once=True and condition='...' for the ones that have these options.
  2. The event name matches exactly (case-sensitive).
  3. The condition returns True (a PeriodicCondition(freq=5) skips four calls out of five).
  4. The registration was not removed, for example consumed by once=True or removed by its own condition: the repr of a removed Subscription that you kept shows active=False.
  5. A handler of the same event ahead of it raised: the next handlers are skipped.

docs.title: KeyError: "key 'epoch' not found in the context; ..."
docs.text: The trigger did not give the key that the handler requires. The message lists the available keys (at most 20 of them). Give the key to the trigger, or read it as an optional value.

docs.title: TypeError: context must be a mapping or None and the keys of data must be str
docs.text: The data of a trigger is a mapping with str keys, such as a dict, given as the second argument: manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}).

docs.title: TypeError about unexpected or positional-only arguments of trigger_event
docs.text: trigger_event and atrigger_event take the event and the context as positional arguments only. Neither trigger_event("epoch_end", epoch=1) nor trigger_event("epoch_end", context=data) is valid: write trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}).

docs.title: TypeError: event must be a str
docs.text: An event is a str, for example a StrEnum member. A member of a plain Enum is not.

docs.title: TypeError: once must be a bool
docs.text: once is True or False. A value that is only truthy or falsy, such as 1 or the string "False", is rejected: convert it first.

docs.title: TypeError: EventManager cannot be copied or pickled and Subscription cannot be ...
docs.text: A manager or a subscription, or an object that holds one, was copied or sent to another process. Create a new manager there and register the handlers, or exclude the manager and the subscriptions from the state of the object.

docs.title: TypeError: ... must take the context as its only required argument
docs.text: The manager cannot call the handler or the condition as f(context), for example a function without parameter, or def f(context=None). Give it one parameter without default, wrap it in a function or a lambda, or bind the extra arguments with functools.partial (see the calling rule).

docs.title: TypeError: ... must not be a generator function
docs.text: Calling a function with yield, or an object whose __call__ has one, runs none of its code. Register a function that iterates over the generator.

docs.title: TypeError: condition must be synchronous and condition ... returned an awaitable
docs.text: The condition is asynchronous: a coroutine function, or an object with async def __call__, is rejected at registration, and a condition that returns an awaitable another way (a lambda that returns a coroutine) fails at the trigger. Compute the value before the trigger and pass it in the payload, or decide inside a coroutine handler.

docs.title: TypeError: ... is a coroutine function; use atrigger_event and ... returned an awaitable
docs.text: A coroutine handler was triggered with trigger_event. Call await manager.atrigger_event(...). For a coroutine function, nothing ran. A handler that returns an awaitable another way (a lambda that returns a coroutine) fails after its call, so the handlers before it have run.

docs.title: subscription.remove() returns False
docs.text: The registration is already removed. This is not an error.

docs.title: Debug
docs.text: minevent does not log. print(manager) shows the number of handlers of each event, and manager.get_subscriptions(event) lists the registrations of an event with the name of each handler and its options. To see the calls and the payload, trace the handlers.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
minevent has three concepts:

  • an event is a string that names something that happens;
  • an event handler is a callable that runs when the event happens;
  • an event manager stores the handlers and triggers the events.

This page shows one example of each feature. The how it works page states the rules of the library, and the examples combine the features. To install it, see Get Started.

docs.title: Register a handler and trigger an event
docs.text:
Create an EventManager, add a handler to an event and trigger the event. A handler is called with the context of the trigger, and _ shows that this one does not use it (see the calling rule):

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def hello_handler(_: Context) -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_end")
Hello!

An event can have several handlers:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda _: print("save the model"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda _: print("send a report"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_end")
save the model
send a report
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'training_end': 2})
>>> manager.events
['training_end']

The decorator on registers a function:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("training_start")
... def log_start(_: Context) -> None:
...     print("start")
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_start")
start

docs.title: Pass data to the handlers
docs.text:
The second argument of trigger_event is the payload, a dict for example. The handlers read it in a Context, with context["key"] for a required value and context.get("key") for an optional one:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context.get('loss', 'unknown')}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 1, loss 0.5
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
epoch 2, loss unknown

The arguments that do not come from the payload can be bound with functools.partial:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def save(path: str, context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"save epoch {context['epoch']} to {path}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(save, "model.pt"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
save epoch 3 to model.pt

docs.title: Control when a handler runs
docs.text:
A condition is a function of the context that returns a boolean, such as PeriodicCondition:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda _: print("checkpoint"), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda _: print("late epoch"),
...     condition=lambda context: context["epoch"] >= 2,
... )
>>> for epoch in range(3):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
checkpoint
checkpoint
late epoch

With once=True, a handler runs at most once:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: print("first epoch"), once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
first epoch
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

docs.title: Remove a handler
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, which removes the registration:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: print("epoch"))
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> subscription.remove()
False
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

A with block scopes a registration, clear_event removes the handlers of an event, and reset removes all the handlers:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda _: print("batch")):
...     manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
batch
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda _: None)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: None)
>>> manager.clear_event("batch_end")
>>> manager.events
['epoch_end']
>>> manager.reset()
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

docs.title: Coroutine handlers
docs.text:
Trigger an event with atrigger_event to await its coroutine handlers. It runs the synchronous handlers too:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def hello_handler(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {context['name']}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda _: print("done"))
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", {"name": "John"}))
Hello John!
done

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An exception of a handler reaches the caller of the trigger, with a note that says which handler raised it:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_loss(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(context["loss"])
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_loss)
>>> try:

docs.title: minevent
docs.text:
Contain the main features of the minevent package.

minevent is a minimal event system with three concepts: an event (a case-sensitive string), a handler (Handler) and an event manager (EventManager) that registers the handlers and triggers the events. A registration returns a Subscription, the handlers and the conditions that take a parameter receive the payload of a trigger in a read-only Context, and a Condition, such as PeriodicCondition, controls when a handler runs.

The package has no dependency, and __version__ is the version of the installed package.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
epoch 3

docs.title: minevent.Context
docs.text:
Bases: Mapping[str, Any]

Implement a read-only mapping of the payload of a trigger.

The data is copied at construction into a private dict, whose keys are checked, and a context has no method that changes it (no __setitem__, update or pop), so neither the code that built the context nor a handler can change what the next handler sees. The values themselves are not copied: a mutable value stays mutable. A context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (with the protocol 2 or higher, like the default one) if its values can.

The values are typed Any: a type checker lets a handler use a value without a cast, and it does not check how the value is used.

context[key] reads a required value and raises a KeyError if it is missing. Its message lists at most 20 of the keys and shortens the long ones. context.get(key, default) reads an optional value. get and key in context do not build the message of that error, so they cost the same for a present key and a missing one, whatever the number of keys. len, iteration, keys, items, values and == behave like those of any collections.abc.Mapping, so dict(context) is a valid **kwargs. A context is equal to a mapping that has the same items, and it is not hashable. The class is final: a type checker reports a subclass.

Name Type Description Default data Mapping[str, object] | None

>>> context["epoch"]

>>> context.get("lr", 0.1)

>>> "loss" in context
True
>>> len(context)
2
>>> context
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})
>>> import copy
>>> copy.deepcopy(context)
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})

docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

add_event_handler registers a handler to an event, a case-sensitive string, and returns the Subscription that removes it. The on decorator registers the function that it decorates. trigger_event and atrigger_event run the handlers of an event in the order they were added, and clear_event and reset remove registrations. events, get_subscriptions and event in manager read the registry, which is thread-safe, and repr shows the number of handlers of each event. >>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda _: print("Hello!"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")

Parameters:

The event name (case-sensitive string).

required handler Handler

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required context Mapping[str, object] | None

None

Type Description TypeError

docs.title: minevent.PeriodicCondition
docs.text:
Implement a periodic condition.

This condition evaluates to True on one call in freq, from the call of index start (the first call has the index 0). It maintains an internal counter that increments with each call. The condition is True when the counter minus start is not negative and is a multiple of freq. With freq=3, start=0 is True on the calls 0, 3 and 6, start=3 skips the first call (3, 6 and 9), and start=2 is True at the end of every third call (2, 5 and 8). With freq=1, it is a warm-up: False for the first start calls and True afterwards.

Note that a call is not idempotent: each call advances the counter, so the condition is stateful. Do not share one instance between several handlers, because they would advance the same counter. The step property reads the counter without advancing it, and reset restarts it. The condition is called with the context of the trigger, like any condition, and ignores it.

The counter is protected by a lock, so every call is counted once, from any number of threads, with and without the GIL. A lock cannot be copied or pickled: a copy of a condition (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy or pickle) starts at the same step, and then has its own counter and lock.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freq int

The frequency (interval) at which the condition evaluates to True. Must be a positive integer.

required start int

The index, from 0, of the first call that evaluates to True. Must be a non-negative integer. Default is 0.

0

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if freq or start is not an integer.

ValueError

if freq is lower than 1, or if start is lower than 0.

Example 
>>> from minevent import Context, PeriodicCondition
>>> context = Context()
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
>>> [condition(context) for _ in range(7)]
[True, False, False, True, False, False, True]
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=3, start=2)
>>> [condition(context) for _ in range(7)]
[False, False, True, False, False, True, False]
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=2)
>>> [condition(context) for _ in range(4)]
[False, False, True, True]
>>> import copy
>>> clone = copy.deepcopy(condition)
>>> clone
PeriodicCondition(freq=1, start=2, step=4)

docs.title: minevent.Subscription
docs.text:
Represent the registration of a handler to an event.

EventManager.add_event_handler returns a subscription: it is the registration itself, so remove removes that registration only, even if the same handler is registered several times. Subscriptions are compared by identity, and copying or pickling one raises a TypeError. A subscription is a context manager: the registration is removed when the with block exits. Its repr shows the event and the name of the handler, then what else decides whether the handler runs: once=True, the name of the condition and active=False if the registration is not in the manager.

The constructor is internal: subscriptions are created by the event manager, and one that is built by hand is not active.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default manager EventManager

The event manager that stores the registration.

required event str

The event name of the registration.

required handler Handler

The registered handler (Handler).

required once bool

If True, the handler runs at most once. Default is False.

False condition Condition | None

The condition evaluated before the handler, or None if the handler always runs. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if EventManager.add_event_handler rejects handler or condition.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def print_epoch(context):
...     print(context["epoch"])
...
>>> def is_late(context):
...     return context["epoch"] >= 2
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda _: None)
>>> subscription
Subscription(event='my_event', handler='<lambda>')
>>> subscription.remove(), subscription.remove()
(True, False)
>>> subscription.active
False
>>> subscription
Subscription(event='my_event', handler='<lambda>', active=False)
>>> manager.add_event_handler("my_event", print_epoch, once=True, condition=is_late)
Subscription(event='my_event', handler='print_epoch', once=True, condition='is_late')
>>> manager.reset()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda _: None):
...     manager
...
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})
>>> manager
EventManager(events={})

docs.title: minevent.calls
docs.text:
Implement how the code of a user is called.

Handler is the type of a handler. validate_signature rejects a handler or a condition that cannot be called with the context, has_kind says if it is a generator or a coroutine function, describe names it, describe_event shows an event name, reject_awaitable rejects the awaitable result of a synchronous call, and add_error_note completes the exception that it raises. These helpers are used by minevent.manager. minevent exports Handler only: the functions are not part of the public API, and can change.

docs.title: minevent.calls.validate_signature
docs.text:
validate_signature(
    func: Callable[..., object], name: str
) -> None

Check that a handler or a condition can be called with the context.

A handler and a condition are always called as func(context). Exactly one parameter must lack a default, and it must be positional: it receives the context. The other parameters keep their default, because the manager never fills them. Names and annotations are not checked. Any other signature is rejected, including *args and **kwargs (they do not say whether the context is expected), and so is a callable whose signature cannot be inspected. A generator function or an async generator function, and a callable object whose __call__ is one (see has_kind), is rejected too, because calling it runs none of its code. The signature is the one that inspect.signature reports: it does not contain the positional arguments that a functools.partial binds, and it is the one of the wrapped function for a decorator that uses functools.wraps. The annotations do not have to be resolvable: on Python 3.14+, a name that is only imported under TYPE_CHECKING is kept as a forward reference instead of raising a NameError. func is not called.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default func Callable[..., object]

The callable to inspect.

required name str

The name of the argument that receives func, used in the error messages.

required

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if func is a generator function or an async generator function (see has_kind), if its signature cannot be inspected, or if it cannot be called with the context as its only argument.

Example 
>>> from minevent.calls import validate_signature
>>> def read_epoch(context):
...     return context["epoch"]
...
>>> validate_signature(read_epoch, "handler")
>>> def train(mode=True): ...
...
>>> validate_signature(train, "handler")
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: handler train must take the context as its only required argument; wrap it in a function or a lambda

Implement the conditions that can be used in the event system.

A condition is any synchronous function that returns a boolean (a lambda, a method or a callable object). It is called before its handler, like a handler: as condition(context) with the read-only Context of the trigger (see minevent.calls.validate_signature). Condition is its type, and EventManager.add_event_handler states how a registration uses it. PeriodicCondition counts its calls. The user guide of the documentation shows how to combine conditions.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "hello", lambda _: print("Hello!"), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("hello")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("hello")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("bye", lambda _: print("Bye!"), condition=lambda _: False)
>>> manager.trigger_event("bye")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda _: print("late epoch"),
...     condition=lambda context: context.get("epoch", 0) >= 2,
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
late epoch

docs.text:
Implement the read-only context passed to the event handlers.

A Context holds the payload of one trigger. It is an immutable mapping from str to values: a handler reads the values it needs and decides what to do when a value is missing.

docs.title: minevent.context.Context
docs.text:
Bases: Mapping[str, Any]

Implement a read-only mapping of the payload of a trigger.

The data is copied at construction into a private dict, whose keys are checked, and a context has no method that changes it (no __setitem__, update or pop), so neither the code that built the context nor a handler can change what the next handler sees. The values themselves are not copied: a mutable value stays mutable. A context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (with the protocol 2 or higher, like the default one) if its values can.

The values are typed Any: a type checker lets a handler use a value without a cast, and it does not check how the value is used.

context[key] reads a required value and raises a KeyError if it is missing. Its message lists at most 20 of the keys and shortens the long ones. context.get(key, default) reads an optional value. get and key in context do not build the message of that error, so they cost the same for a present key and a missing one, whatever the number of keys. len, iteration, keys, items, values and == behave like those of any collections.abc.Mapping, so dict(context) is a valid **kwargs. A context is equal to a mapping that has the same items, and it is not hashable. The class is final: a type checker reports a subclass.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Mapping[str, object] | None

The mapping to copy, or None for an empty context. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if data is neither None nor a mapping, or if a key of data is not a str.

Example 
>>> from minevent import Context
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
>>> context["epoch"]
3
>>> context.get("lr", 0.1)
0.1
>>> "loss" in context
True
>>> len(context)
2
>>> context
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})
>>> import copy
>>> copy.deepcopy(context)
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})

docs.title: minevent.manager
docs.text:
Implement the event manager and the subscriptions.

EventManager stores the registrations of the handlers and triggers the events, and Subscription is the registration of one handler to one event. The conditions of a registration are in minevent.conditions.

docs.title: minevent.manager.EventManager
docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

add_event_handler registers a handler to an event, a case-sensitive string, and returns the Subscription that removes it. The on decorator registers the function that it decorates. trigger_event and atrigger_event run the handlers of an event in the order they were added, and clear_event and reset remove registrations. events, get_subscriptions and event in manager read the registry, which is thread-safe, and repr shows the number of handlers of each event. A manager is always truthy and has no length. Copying or pickling it raises a TypeError. The guarantees and the limits are in the "How It Works" page of the documentation, and the reasons in its "Design Choices" page.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda _: print("Hello!"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'my_event': 1})

docs.text:
add_event_handler(
    event: str,
    handler: Handler,
    *,
    once: bool = False,
    condition: Condition | None = None,
) -> Subscription

Add a handler to an event.

Each trigger of the event calls the handler after the handlers added before it, as handler(context) with the read-only Context of the trigger. minevent.calls.validate_signature states which signatures are accepted.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string).

required handler Handler

The callable to attach to the event (Handler).

required once bool

If True, the registration is removed just before the first call of the handler, so it runs at most once, even when several threads trigger the event. A condition that is False does not consume it. Default is False.

False condition Condition | None

A synchronous function that returns a boolean, called like a handler before it: the handler runs only if the result is true. A stateful condition, such as PeriodicCondition, must not be shared between registrations. If None, the handler always runs. Default is None.

None

Returns:

Type Description Subscription

A subscription whose remove method removes this registration only.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if handler is not callable, if condition is neither None nor callable, if once is not a bool, if handler or condition is a generator function, cannot be called with the context as its only argument, or has a signature that cannot be inspected, or if condition is a coroutine function. A callable object is judged by its __call__. The manager is unchanged.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2),
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda _: print("first"), once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 0})
epoch 0
first
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
epoch 2

Run the handlers of an event, awaiting the coroutine handlers.

It behaves like trigger_event, but the awaitable that a handler returns is awaited before the next handler. A synchronous handler blocks the event loop while it runs. The registrations and the context are read when the coroutine starts to run, not when it is created (see the "Limits" of the "How It Works" page of the documentation).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required context Mapping[str, object] | None

The data of the trigger, as in trigger_event. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if context is neither None nor a mapping with str keys, or if a condition returns an awaitable (a condition is never awaited). Any exception of a handler or a condition also propagates.

Example

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> async def hello_handler(context):
...     print(f"Hello {context['name']}!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", {"name": "John"}))
Hello John!
